text: Charles Bentley (1805/6–4 September 1854) was an English watercolour painter known for his coastal and river scenery. Born in 1805 or 1806, he was the son of a master-carpenter and builder residing in Tottenham Court Road, London. He began working on colouring prints for Theodore Fielding and was eventually apprenticed to him to learn aquatinting. During this time, he was sent to Paris, likely to assist with the plates for *Excursion sur les Cotes et dans les Ports de Normandie* (Paris, 1823–5), most of which were based on watercolours by Richard Bonington. After completing his apprenticeship, Bentley earned some income through engraving or designing plates for periodicals but gradually shifted focus to painting watercolours. He exhibited four works at the first Exhibition of the New Society of Painters in Water-Colours (later the Royal Institute of Painters in Water-Colours) in 1832 and six the following year. He lived at 15, Bateman's Buildings, on the south side of Soho Square, where he resided for six years. In February 1834, he was elected an Associate-Exhibitor of the Old Water-Colour Society (later the Royal Society of Painters in Water-Colours). By 1838, he had moved to 11, Mornington Place, Hampstead Road, where he remained except for a three-year period when he lived with William Callow in Charlotte Street. His 1838 exhibitions included two imaginative compositions: *From the Red Rover*, depicting a naval battle, and *From Tom Cringle's Log*, showing a sinking slave-ship. He first exhibited at the British Institution in 1843 and became a full member of the Old Society the next year. In 1851, he exhibited at the Society of British Artists. Bentley painted scenes throughout Britain, in Jersey, the north of Ireland, and Normandy, which he visited multiple times with Callow between 1836 and 1841. He also exhibited views of Venice, Holland, and Düsseldorf, though it is uncertain whether he visited these places, as some works—such as those of Trebizond and Abydos, shown in 1841 and 1849—were based on drawings by Coke Smyth. He also prepared illustrations for *12 Views in the Interior of Guiana*, published by Rudolf Ackermann in 1841, using studies from an expedition to South America led by John Morison. Bentley was not financially successful; Samuel Redgrave described him as "uncertain in his transactions, and always poor." He died of cholera on 4 September 1854, leaving a widow, and was buried in the western side of Highgate Cemetery. The grave (no. 6056) no longer has a headstone or marker.
